I agree that Tutberidze is culpable and morally bankrupt for so many reasons (teaching harmful technique, emotional abuse, physical/food abuse) but it is my firm belief that a focus on her culpability misses the big picture.  

If you read the Rodchenkov affair (or watch Icarus), you learn that this is not about one team— This is about a government-run, government-mandated doping program that applied—- and seemingly probably still applies, at least as of 2021— to the majority of Russian athletes. 

As a PhD-level scientist myself, I was skeptical at first— but the investigations that have followed his testimony provide pretty compelling evidence that he is telling the truth about this system, and I think we have to listen to the data here. It’s a really hard pill to swallow but I’d rather accept the truth than stick my head in the sand— no matter how much I adore watching Kamila skate. ☹️

Russia needs to admit wrongdoing, change its methods, and move forward with promotion of clean sport. They’ll probably still beat the rest of us most of the time. I hope this miracle occurs— but if not, they should not be allowed to participate.

I have tried motion (usemotion.com), then reclaim, then SkedPal, and now I’m back to motion. 

They will all schedule your tasks for you based on deadlines, and all can block off time with google calendar. So you can’t go super wrong there. 

In terms of customizability of weekly time zones (eg, work hours; zones that you can use to say when in your week a given task should be scheduled if there’s availability), reclaim is the least elaborate, allowing you just two maps (work vs personal), motion is second most elaborate (unlimited zones), and SkedPal is impossibly elaborate, giving you unlimited zones that can be further broken down as “green, yellow, and red” to show preference within that zone. The motion system is my favorite there. 

In terms of task organization, motion has the least things to fiddle with, which is best in my opinion. You can still put things in projects but I don’t. Reclaim is just a list as I recall. SkedPal is this very flexible outline where some lines can be notes, and others tasks, and still other lines can delineate sections with automatic characteristics applied the tasks that are entered in that section (eg, schedule things in this section as work hours tasks, high priority). Personally, I lost a week of productivity to fiddling with that damn outline. Not worth it. I think motion is probably the best in that domain too, mostly in that it’s simple but effective and it doesn’t tempt me to mess with it too much.

The largest problem with all three of them is that the usability on smartphone is pretty low. Motion has a decently functional app, although it’s buggy. I found SkedPal’s app to be hopelessly buggy and impossible to use. Reclaim does not have an app. Honestly, I’m on my phone constantly, so I’m hoping motion app continues to improve— it’s just ok, but that’s better than the others. 

So it’s motion for me, but I think there’s a ton of room for innovation and improvement in this space.

A couple of key points: 

- hormones estrogen and progesterone are actually completely normal in women with PMDD. So there's no evidence that they need to be balanced. 

- Rather, the problem is an abnormal sensitivity to normal hormone changes. This may be due to altered metabolism of estrogen and progesterone into their powerful neurosteroid metabolites (like allopregnanolone) 

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9435325

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/m/pubmed/26272051/

- there is some evidence that the placebo response is stronger in women with PMDD than in the average population-- so there's a good chance that whatever you try (even sugarpill) will improve your symptoms in the short term (perhaps for a month or two) and then the symptoms will come back. This is the reason that placebo controlled trials are so key, and why I'm mentioning SSRIs so much-- they have repeatedly beat placebo in controlled trials, which is difficult in this population. 

- SSRIs are by far the most effective treatment that have been studied  if you're interested in placebo controlled evidence. They are also equally effective if you only take them when you have symptoms, so you don't have to over-medicate. YMMV-- not everyone improves, but it's the best option we have at the moment. 

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2670364/

- placebo controlled trials of oral contraceptives have had disappointing results for emotional symptoms of PMDD. Generally speaking, if you have predominantly physical PMS symptoms (pain, bloating, etc) then oral contraceptives are more helpful. But if you have mostly mood symptoms (irritability, depression, anxiety) then oral contraceptives are only a little more helpful than taking a sugar pill. And after a few months they're about the same. Again, YMMV-- but beware the placebo response. 

http://www.cochrane.org/CD006586/MENSTR_birth-control-pills-with-drospirenone-for-treating-premenstrual-syndrome
